name: Polonium
blurb: No MR application. 209Po is the only polonium nuclide that combines I > 0 with a half-life long enough to contemplate an experiment, and its magnetic moment is tabulated to two figures; polonium work is alpha containment, not spectroscopy.
mrNotes: 210Po, the isotope of practical and forensic concern, is even-even with I = 0 and a 138 d half-life.
No polonium NMR signal has ever been reported, and the bulk susceptibility of the metal is not established.

isotopes.notes: Moment +0.68 muN is quoted to two significant figures in the Stone-derived tables, so the derived gamma of 10.37 MHz/T carries the same 1 percent uncertainty. Half-life revised from 102 y to about 124 y.

name: Astatine
blurb: No MR application. Astatine belongs to nuclear medicine, not magnetic resonance: 211At (7.2 h) is an alpha emitter in clinical targeted alpha therapy trials, and no weighable sample of the element has ever existed.
mrNotes: 211At decay emits 77 to 92 keV polonium K X-rays, so dosimetry is done on a gamma camera; MR contributes nothing to its detection.
Bulk properties including magnetic susceptibility are unmeasured; the largest quantities ever produced are nanogram scale.

isotopes.notes: Ground state spin 9/2 is established from nuclear structure data, but no magnetic moment is adopted in the Stone-derived tables, so gamma is left null rather than guessed.

name: Radon
blurb: No MR application and no useful NMR isotope. 222Rn, the isotope that matters for dosimetry and geology, is even-even with I = 0, and the odd-A radon nuclides are short-lived alpha emitters.
mrNotes: There is no radon analogue of hyperpolarized 129Xe or 3He: no radon isotope offers spin 1/2 with a usable lifetime and a way to make grams of it.
222Rn has a 3.82 d half-life and decays by 5.49 MeV alpha emission.

name: Francium
blurb: No MR application. The longest-lived francium isotope, 223Fr, decays in 22 minutes, so francium exists only as clouds of trapped atoms; there has never been a sample to put in a magnet.
mrNotes: Francium hyperfine structure is measured by laser trapping and optical spectroscopy on thousands of atoms, which is many orders of magnitude below any NMR detection limit.

name: Radium
blurb: No MR application. Radium's medical role is radiotherapy: radium needles historically, and today 223Ra dichloride for bone metastases of castration resistant prostate cancer. 226Ra, the 1600 y isotope, is even-even with I = 0.
mrNotes: Radium is a calcium mimic and deposits at sites of active bone turnover, which is what makes 223Ra bone seeking without a carrier molecule.
223Ra has I = 3/2 and mu = +0.2705 muN from collinear resonance ionization spectroscopy at ISOLDE, but it is dosed at kilobecquerel per kilogram levels, far below any NMR sensitivity.

isotopes.notes: Alpha emitter used clinically as 223RaCl2. Magnetic moment from laser spectroscopy; the spectroscopic quadrupole moment is not adopted here, so q is left null. No NMR observation exists.

name: Actinium
blurb: No MR application. Actinium matters as 225Ac (9.92 d), the alpha emitter in 225Ac-PSMA-617 and related targeted alpha therapies; what counts there is its four-alpha decay chain, not its nuclear spin.
mrNotes: 225Ac has I = 3/2 but no adopted magnetic moment, so no gamma can honestly be quoted for it.
227Ac (21.8 y) is the actinium isotope in the nuclear moment tables, with mu = +1.22 muN and Q = +170 fm2.

isotopes.notes: Targeted alpha therapy nuclide. Spin 3/2 is established; magnetic moment not tabulated, so gamma is null.
Moment and quadrupole moment from the Stone-derived EasySpin table; quoted to three and two figures respectively.

name: Thorium
blurb: No MR application. Natural thorium is effectively pure 232Th, which is even-even with I = 0, so there is no thorium NMR to do. Its MR-adjacent history is Thorotrast, a colloidal 232ThO2 X-ray contrast agent used from the 1930s to the 1950s that caused hepatic angiosarcoma decades after injection.
mrNotes: 229Th (7917 y) has I = 5/2, mu = +0.360(7) muN and Q = +311 fm2; it carries the 8.4 eV isomer being developed as a nuclear clock.
227Th (18.7 d) is the alpha emitter in targeted thorium conjugates now in early phase oncology trials.

Thorium metal is a temperature-independent Pauli paramagnet; high-purity metal gives chi_g = +0.41e-6 cm3/g at 300 K, i.e. chi_m near +96e-6 cm3/mol, below the older tabulated +132e-6 used here for consistency.

isotopes.notes: Moment and quadrupole moment from the 2013 reanalysis of the laser spectroscopy, mu = +0.360(7) muN and Q = +3.11(6) barn; these supersede the older +0.46 muN and +4.3 barn still carried in the EasySpin table.

name: Protactinium
blurb: No MR application, although on paper 231Pa is a respectable nucleus: I = 3/2, gamma = 10.1 MHz/T and a single naturally occurring isotope give a receptivity near 390 times 13C. It is also a 32,760 y alpha emitter available in milligram amounts at best, which settles the matter.
mrNotes: Protactinium occurs in nature only as trace 231Pa in uranium ores; the 100 percent abundance here is its isotopic composition, not a bulk availability.
231Pa is the one entry in the Stone-derived EasySpin table printed without a sign on mu, meaning the sign of the moment is not experimentally established.
Q = -170 fm2 with I = 3/2 would broaden any site lacking cubic symmetry.

isotopes.notes: Sign of the moment is not established; the positive sign here follows the convention of the source table. Abundance is the isotopic composition of naturally occurring protactinium.

name: Uranium
blurb: Not an MR material. 235U is NMR active with I = 7/2, but it combines the worst of everything: gamma = -0.83 MHz/T, 0.72 percent abundance and Q = +494 fm2, giving a receptivity of 0.0065 relative to 13C. It has been detected only in ordered solids such as UO2 and USb2, where large internal hyperfine fields supply the field.
mrNotes: At 3 T the 235U Larmor frequency is 2.5 MHz, lower than the 1H frequency of a 60 mT extremity scanner.
238U and 234U, which together are over 99 percent of natural uranium, are even-even with I = 0.
Uranium metal is weakly paramagnetic, chi_m about +399e-6 cm3/mol; embedded depleted uranium fragments are a chemical and radiological question, not an MR force or heating question.

isotopes.notes: Moment -0.38(3) muN and Q = +4.936 barn from the Stone-derived table. Observed by NMR only in magnetically ordered or itinerant 5f solids; no solution spectrum exists.

name: Neptunium
blurb: No MR application. 237Np (2.14 My) has I = 5/2 and mu = +3.16 muN, one of the largest actinide moments, but it exists only in reprocessing streams and research quantities.
mrNotes: Neptunium hyperfine fields are measured by 237Np Mossbauer spectroscopy on the 59.5 keV transition rather than by NMR.
Q = +387 fm2 with I = 5/2 makes any non-cubic site extremely broad.

isotopes.notes: Moment and quadrupole moment from the Stone-derived EasySpin table.

name: Plutonium
blurb: Not an MR material, but 239Pu is a genuine NMR nucleus: spin 1/2, gamma = 3.08 MHz/T, first observed in 2012 in PuO2 at 4 K by sweeping the field from 3 to 8 T after roughly fifty years of failed searches.
mrNotes: Yasuoka et al., Science 336, 901 (2012); the signal needs the hyperfine enhancement of an ordered 5f system, not a diamagnetic solution.
Plutonium metal has a large temperature-independent susceptibility near +5.3e-4 cm3/mol with no ordered local moment.
239Pu is a 24,110 y alpha emitter; any experiment is glovebox and double-containment work.

isotopes.notes: Spin 1/2, so no quadrupole broadening; the difficulty is the small moment and the containment, not the linewidth.

name: Americium
blurb: No MR application. 243Am (7370 y) has I = 5/2 and mu = +1.52 muN; americium's practical use is as a sealed source, most familiar as 241Am emitting 59.5 keV gammas.
mrNotes: 241Am (432.6 y) is the smoke detector and calibration source isotope and was the 59.5 keV photon source in early single-photon bone absorptiometry.
Am3+ is 5f6 with J = 0, so americium compounds show only weak, nearly temperature-independent Van Vleck paramagnetism.

isotopes.notes: Moment and quadrupole moment from the Stone-derived EasySpin table; 241Am has the same spin but is not tabulated there.

name: Curium
blurb: No MR application. Cm3+ is 5f7 with S = 7/2, the actinide analogue of Gd3+, so it is strongly paramagnetic in principle; in practice every isotope is an intense alpha emitter and no curium chelate will ever be injected as a relaxation agent.
mrNotes: Curium speciation is followed by Cm3+ luminescence and by EPR; no NMR of a curium nucleus has been reported.
244Cm (18.1 y) is the alpha source in the alpha particle X-ray spectrometers flown on Mars rovers.

name: Berkelium
blurb: No MR application. Berkelium has never been produced in more than microgram amounts; its recent role was as the 249Bk target used to synthesize tennessine.
mrNotes: 249Bk (330 d) is the isotope available for chemistry, in tens of micrograms, and it decays into 249Cf during the experiment.

name: Californium
blurb: No MR application. Californium's practical isotope, 252Cf, is a spontaneous fission neutron source used for neutron brachytherapy, neutron radiography and reactor startup, and it is even-even with I = 0.
mrNotes: One microgram of 252Cf emits about 2.3e6 neutrons per second, which is why it is handled as a source rather than as a chemical.

name: Einsteinium
blurb: No MR application. Einsteinium is made in nanogram quantities; a 2021 coordination chemistry study worked with roughly 200 ng of 254Es.
mrNotes: Self-irradiation damages the sample and its lattice during the measurement, which rules out any experiment needing hours of signal averaging.

name: Fermium
blurb: No MR application. 257Fm has a 100.5 d half-life but fermium has never been isolated in bulk; its chemistry is done on tracer quantities of ions.
mrNotes: The magnetism entry is inferred from the 5f12 configuration; no bulk sample has ever been weighed, so chi is unknown.

name: Mendelevium
blurb: No MR application. Mendelevium chemistry is done atom at a time; even 258Md, with a 51.5 d half-life, has only ever been made in quantities of about a million atoms.
mrNotes: The magnetism entry is inferred from the 5f13 configuration; there is no bulk sample and no susceptibility measurement.

name: Nobelium
blurb: No MR application. Nobelium is notable for its unusually stable 2+ state, a consequence of the filled 5f14 shell, and for being studied a few atoms at a time.
mrNotes: A filled 5f shell implies no local 4f-type moment, but nothing about bulk nobelium has been measured; the magnetism entry is an inference.

name: Lawrencium
blurb: No MR application. The state of the art for lawrencium is the 2015 measurement of its first ionization energy, 4.96 eV, made on a handful of 256Lr atoms.
mrNotes: The magnetism entry is inferred from a closed 5f14 shell plus one loosely bound valence electron; no bulk property has been measured.

name: Rutherfordium
blurb: No MR application. Rutherfordium's longest-lived isotope, 267Rf, survives on the order of an hour, and its chemistry is done one atom at a time as a group 4 homologue of hafnium.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are inferred from hafnium and zirconium; nothing bulk has been measured.

name: Dubnium
blurb: No MR application. 268Db lives about a day, long by superheavy standards, and has been shown chemically to behave as a group 5 homologue of tantalum.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are inferred from tantalum and niobium; no sample exists to measure a susceptibility on.

name: Seaborgium
blurb: No MR application. Seaborgium isotopes live minutes at most; gas-phase chemistry has confirmed it forms a volatile oxychloride like molybdenum and tungsten.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are inferred from tungsten; total production is a few hundred atoms.

name: Bohrium
blurb: No MR application. Bohrium has been characterized chemically from about six atoms of 267Bh, forming a volatile oxychloride as expected for a rhenium homologue.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are inferred from rhenium; no bulk sample has ever existed.

name: Hassium
blurb: No MR application. Hassium isotopes live seconds; the element was identified chemically through volatile HsO4, mirroring osmium tetroxide.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are inferred from osmium; fewer than a hundred atoms have been made.

name: Meitnerium
blurb: No MR application. Meitnerium has never been isolated in chemically usable form; its isotopes decay in seconds and its chemistry remains unstudied.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from iridium, not measurements.

name: Darmstadtium
blurb: No MR application. Darmstadtium was first made in 1994 at GSI; its longest-lived known isotope decays in seconds and no chemistry has been done.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from platinum, not measurements.

name: Roentgenium
blurb: No MR application. Roentgenium isotopes live a couple of minutes at most and only a few dozen atoms have ever been produced.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from gold, which is itself diamagnetic; nothing has been measured.

name: Copernicium
blurb: No MR application. Copernicium is predicted to be extremely volatile, possibly a gas at room temperature, and 285Cn decays in about half a minute.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from mercury and from relativistic calculations, not measurements.

name: Nihonium
blurb: No MR application. Nihonium was first made at RIKEN in 2004 and named in 2016; its isotopes decay in seconds and it has only ever existed as single atoms.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from thallium; no measurement exists.

name: Flerovium
blurb: No MR application. Flerovium isotopes live a few seconds; adsorption experiments suggest a volatile metal with weak surface binding.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from lead and from relativistic calculations, not measurements.

name: Moscovium
blurb: No MR application. Moscovium isotopes decay in well under a second and only a few dozen atoms have ever been detected.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from bismuth; no measurement exists.

name: Livermorium
blurb: No MR application. Livermorium isotopes decay in tens of milliseconds; the element has only ever existed as a few dozen atoms recorded in a detector.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from polonium; no measurement exists.

name: Tennessine
blurb: No MR application. Tennessine was made by bombarding a 249Bk target with 48Ca; its isotopes decay in tens of milliseconds.
mrNotes: Category and magnetism are predictions from astatine, itself barely characterized; no measurement exists.

name: Oganesson
blurb: No MR application. Oganesson is the heaviest element made to date, with 294Og decaying in about 0.7 ms; only a handful of atoms have ever been observed.
mrNotes: Predicted to be a solid rather than a noble gas because of relativistic effects; the magnetism entry is an inference from a closed 7p shell.
